# Abstract {#sec-abstract}

*Background*: Fantasy football performance can be streaky, and managers often wonder whether early-season production predicts how players will perform later in the year.

*Method*: Using the *player_stats_weekly* dataset from Petersen, I selected all QBs from the 2015–2024 seasons, split their games into Weeks 1–8 and Weeks 9–17, and calculated each player’s average fantasy points and games played in each segment. I then summarized the overall averages to compare early vs. late-season performance.

*Results*: Across 502 player-seasons, players averaged about 5.1 games and 12.7 fantasy points in Weeks 1–8, and about 5.6 games and 12.9 fantasy points in Weeks 9–17. On average, this indicates only a very small increase in both opportunity (games played) and fantasy production later in the season.

*Discussion*: : These results suggest that, for most QBs, fantasy performance is relatively stable across the season rather than dramatically improving or collapsing in the second half. This stability means that early “breakouts” and “slumps” may often reflect short-term variance rather than true changes in player ability or role.

*Conclusion*: Overall, early-season performance for QBs from 2015–2024 was a reasonable but not explosive indicator of late-season performance, with only slight average increases in games and points. Fantasy managers should be cautious about overreacting to small early-season sample sizes and instead consider a player’s full-season context when making decisions.


# Background {#sec-background}

Fantasy football performance is inherently streaky: some players start hot and fade, while others heat up late in the season. Looking only at full-season averages can hide these trends and make it hard to know whether a player is truly improving or just having a few lucky games. Because we have weekly fantasy points across an entire season, we can treat them as a time series and compare early-season performance to late-season performance. This helps managers see which players may be “second-half risers” or “early-season mirages.”

## Research Question

Do NFL players tend to score more fantasy points in the second half of the season (Weeks 9–17) than in the first half (Weeks 1–8), and which players show the biggest improvements or declines over time?

## Hypothesis

I hypothesize that players who score higher than the league-wide average in the first half of the season (Weeks 1–8) will tend to do even better in the later weeks (Weeks 9–17). In other words, early high scorers will, on average, either maintain or increase their fantasy production over time, while players who are below average early in the season will be less likely to show big late-season improvements.

## Justification

This hypothesis follows from the idea of autocorrelation and time‐series patterns described in Chapter 25: past values of a series are often related to future values. If a player is consistently scoring above the league-wide average in Weeks 1–8, that suggests a strong role, good health, and favorable usage, which are likely to continue into later weeks. In time-series terms, we expect some “momentum,” so high early-season values should predict equal or higher values later in the season.

# Method {#sec-method}

I used the *player_stats_weekly dataset* from the textbook provided by *Petersen*, which contains weekly fantasy points for NFL players. To make this more simple to look at and a test to see data, I have taken a small portion of players. This portion include all QBs between the years of 2015 and 2024. We have the last ten seasons. The weeks have been divided up from Week 1 through 8, and then Week 9 through 17. 18 is not included because before the 2021 season, every team got a 17th game. Doing it this way would counteract injuries in the first few years of the findings versus the byes that teams have, and then wouldn't skew results from players later down the road having an extra game.

# Results {#sec-results}

## Code
```{r}
target_season <- max(player_stats_weekly$season, na.rm = TRUE)

player_stats_weekly %>%
  filter(
    position == "QB",
    season >= 2015,
    season <= 2024,
    !is.na(player_display_name)
  ) %>%
  distinct(player_display_name) %>%
  arrange(player_display_name) %>%
  print(n = Inf)


early_late_by_player <- player_stats_weekly %>%
  filter(
    season == target_season,
    !is.na(fantasyPoints),
    week >= 1, week <= 17
  ) %>%
  group_by(player_id, player_display_name, position, team) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_1_8  = mean(fantasyPoints[week %in% 1:8],  na.rm = TRUE),
    games_1_8 = sum(week %in% 1:8  & !is.na(fantasyPoints)),
    mean_9_17  = mean(fantasyPoints[week %in% 9:17], na.rm = TRUE),
    games_9_17 = sum(week %in% 9:17 & !is.na(fantasyPoints)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%

  filter(games_1_8 > 0, games_9_17 > 0) %>%
  mutate(
    diff = mean_9_17 - mean_1_8,
    direction = dplyr::case_when(
      diff > 0  ~ "improved",
      diff < 0  ~ "declined",
      TRUE      ~ "no_change"
    )
  )

early_late_by_player %>%
  filter(position == "QB") %>%
  arrange(desc(diff))

early_late_by_player %>%
  filter(position == "QB") %>%
  arrange(diff)



early_late_by_player %>%
  arrange(desc(diff)) %>%
  head(195)

early_late_by_player %>%
  arrange(diff) %>%
  head(195)
```

## Findings

Across 502 player-seasons, players averaged about 5.1 games in Weeks 1–8 and 5.6 games in Weeks 9–17, and their average fantasy points were 12.73 early vs 12.89 late.

## Visualization
```{r}
early_late_qb <- player_stats_weekly %>%
  filter(
    position == "QB",
    season >= 2015, season <= 2024,
    !is.na(fantasyPoints),
    week >= 1, week <= 17
  ) %>%
  group_by(season, player_id, player_display_name, team) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_1_8   = mean(fantasyPoints[week %in% 1:8],  na.rm = TRUE),
    games_1_8  = sum(week %in% 1:8  & !is.na(fantasyPoints)),
    mean_9_17  = mean(fantasyPoints[week %in% 9:17], na.rm = TRUE),
    games_9_17 = sum(week %in% 9:17 & !is.na(fantasyPoints)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(games_1_8 > 0, games_9_17 > 0) %>%
  mutate(diff = mean_9_17 - mean_1_8)

ggplot(
  data = early_late_qb,
  mapping = aes(x = mean_1_8, y = mean_9_17)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    x = "Average Fantasy Points (Weeks 1–8)",
    y = "Average Fantasy Points (Weeks 9–17)",
    title = "QB Fantasy Performance: Early vs Late Season",
    subtitle = "Seasons 2015–2024; points above the line improved later in the year"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

The dots form a strong upward diagonal, so QBs who scored a lot early generally also scored a lot later, early performance does predict late performance.

# Strengths and Limitations {#sec-strengthsAndLimitations}

*Strengths*: Summarizing players with means and differences, plus a scatterplot of early vs. late averages, makes it straightforward to see who improved, who declined, and how stable performance is across the season. This also creates a definitive idea of analyzing the consistent players in the league, if they score the average line, we could say they could continue to do that, relaibility over potential "booming."

*Limitations*: However, this study also has several limitations. First, I only looked at fantasy points and did not control for important factors like injuries, changes in team role, strength of schedule, or bye weeks, which can all affect late-season scoring. Second, the cutoff at Week 8 is somewhat arbitrary; a different cutoff (for example, quarters of the season) might show a slightly different pattern.


# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

On average, players in this sample played a similar number of games in the first half (about 5.1 games) and second half (about 5.6 games) of the season, and their mean fantasy points were also very close (about 12.7 points in Weeks 1–8 vs. 12.9 points in Weeks 9–17). This pattern suggests that, for most players, fantasy performance is fairly stable across the year, with only small average changes between early and late weeks. In practical terms, early-season stars do not always explode even more later, and early slow starts do not always lead to huge second-half breakouts; fantasy managers should be cautious about overreacting to short streaks and instead consider a player’s overall role and context
